questions.q: Label the object: 'The teacher praised the diligent student.'
questions.a: 'the diligent student' — receives the praising. A wrong answer 'teacher' shows subject-object confusion; 'praised' alone shows verb-object confusion.

questions.q: 'The sky turned grey.' Is 'grey' an object or a complement — and why?
questions.a: Complement — 'turned' here is a being-verb (became); 'grey' describes the sky's state, nothing receives an action. A wrong answer 'object' reveals the everything-after-verb-is-object habit.

questions.q: Which verb is intransitive (no object possible): 'She slept' / 'She ate' / 'She read'?
questions.a: 'slept' — you cannot 'sleep something'; 'ate' and 'read' can take objects. A wrong answer reveals the student hasn't split verbs into transitive vs intransitive.

questions.q: Inside a sentence, nouns do different jobs: subject (does the action), object (receives it), and complement (completes ______ — 'She is a DOCTOR').
Fill in the blank: Inside a sentence, nouns do different jobs: subject (does the action), object (receives it), and ______ (completes being-verbs — 'She is a DOCTOR').
Fill in the blank: Now 'Ravi is a doctor' — 'a doctor' is not kicked, not acted upon; it renames Ravi — ______.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student labels subject, verb, object, and complement in simple sentences, distinguishes objects from complements (after being-verbs there is no object), and identifies transitive vs intransitive verbs.
